bridges.description: Show that Christian explanations can adequately reconcile suffering with divine goodness and power.
Explain why responsible freedom, consequential choice, and character formation can require permitted suffering.
Explain how creator authority, victim benefit, biblical diversity, incarnation, redemption, and heaven form a morally adequate account.
Connect the explanation to the duty and privilege of relieving suffering.
Show that the Christian explanations offered do not adequately account for the scale and kinds of suffering.
Test freedom, character, and usefulness explanations against victims, natural evil, and lives lacking overall benefit.
Argue that conflicting biblical accounts and failed imminent expectations weaken explanatory adequacy.
Distinguish unsatisfying explanation from the practical human response of reducing suffering.

sections.title: Coherence and responsible agency
sections.rationale: Establishes the logical framework and central claim that consequential responsibility can make permitted suffering possible.

sections.title: Natural evil and victim benefit
sections.rationale: Tests adequacy against disasters, starving children, involuntary usefulness, and whether victims receive sufficient benefit.

sections.title: Biblical diversity and conflict
sections.rationale: Tests whether varied biblical explanations are complementary or conflict at the level of causal responsibility.

sections.title: Incarnation, intervention, and kingdom
sections.rationale: Tests whether Christ's suffering, redemption, resurrection, and kingdom expectations answer apparent nonintervention.

sections.title: Practical response, heaven, and final choice
sections.rationale: Preserves both final summaries on action, heaven, moral formation, and the claimed value of a painful life.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: The claims that God is all-powerful, God is all-loving, and suffering exists appear inconsistent unless a premise is denied or an adequate extenuating circumstance is supplied.
moves.warrant: An all-powerful God could prevent suffering and an all-loving God would not want it, yet suffering exists; proposed resolutions either limit an attribute or explain coexistence.
moves.inference: Christianity bears an explanatory burden beyond merely repeating the three propositions.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Contains Ehrman's full three-proposition formulation, both resolution strategies, and his first biblical example without relying on host framing.
moves.attributionRationale: The host hands the floor to Ehrman and his exposition continues until the next named handoff.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Speaker identity and the central formulation are clear in the canonical events.
moves.importanceRationale: States the critic's motion-level explanatory test.

burdenContact.rationale: Defines what an adequate Christian explanation must reconcile.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.claim: Divine omnipotence means power to do anything logically possible, and some valuable states cannot logically be achieved without allowing suffering.
moves.warrant: Contradictory descriptions name no possible action; unlike a surgeon's physical limits, God's constraint is logical, and certain goods depend on possible evil.
moves.inference: The three propositions can be compatible once omnipotence and the conditions of goods are stated precisely.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Swinburne's direct answer and ends after his physical-versus-logical distinction and statement that some goods require permitted evil.

moves.speaker: Richard Swinburne
moves.claim: Free and responsible choice is valuable because others' welfare can genuinely depend on us, while creator authority is conditioned on victims receiving an overall beneficial life or other benefits.
moves.warrant: Responsibility is real only when choices have consequences; parents may authorize painful treatment because they nurture children, and God is the source of existence and possible goods.
moves.inference: Permitting consequential freedom may be within divine rights, but only under the stated victim-benefit condition.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Runs from responsible freedom through parental and creator authority to the explicit condition of an on-balance beneficial life and compensating benefits.
